name: Mirror checking / mirror avoidance
lead: Mirror checking and mirror avoidance are two opposite habits around reflective surfaces. Checking means looking at one's appearance repeatedly to inspect skin, hair, facial features or outfit, which many people do as part of grooming and getting ready. Avoidance means steering clear of mirrors, for example covering them or skipping them when dressing. In clinical writing both are described as appearance-related behaviors that can accompany body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) [1][2].

For someone working on how they look, the mirror is the basic feedback tool: it is how skin, grooming, expressions and outfits get reviewed before leaving the house. The research literature adds that how often and how long one checks matters. Wikipedia lists repetitive appearance checking, outfit changing and excessive grooming among BDD behaviors, and notes that some people instead avoid mirrors [1]. Clinicians call checking, grooming and similar habits appearance-related safety behaviors [3].

In looksmaxxing communities the terms appear in discussions of self-assessment and appearance anxiety. Research on the behaviors sits mainly within the BDD and body-image literature, where cognitive behavioral therapy with exposure and ritual prevention addresses them [1][2].

angle.text: Brief, purposeful mirror use is how people review grooming, skin and clothing and make small corrections. Researchers describe a pattern of repeated or avoidant mirror behavior that is tied to appearance distress, which is where the clinical literature on checking and avoidance applies [1][3].

infobox: CBT with exposure and ritual prevention [1][2]

paras: Wikipedia describes mirror checking as one of several repetitive behaviors in BDD, alongside comparing oneself with others, changing outfits, excessive grooming, restricting eating, and camouflaging the perceived flaw with makeup or clothing. The same article says some people with BDD instead avoid mirrors [1].

A 2017 clinical review describes BDD as a preoccupation with perceived flaws that are not noticeable to others, with associated repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking. The disorder generally begins in adolescence and is often underdiagnosed [2]. Standard treatments are summarised in a 2021 consensus article [5]. Wikipedia reports that people with BDD may spend hours a day preoccupied with the perceived flaw [1].

Recommended treatments for BDD include cognitive behavioral therapy and SSRI antidepressants [1][2]. BDD-specific CBT manuals include exposure and ritual prevention, cognitive restructuring and perceptual retraining, as described by Wikipedia in reference to work by Sabine Wilhelm and colleagues [1]. A 2011 review notes that the disorder often centres on the face, such as the nose or skin [6].

Research on mirror exposure has been conducted in related groups. A 2026 study of people with body dysmorphic symptoms reported that body satisfaction improved from a first mirror session to a second but not within one session [4].

A 2020 randomised trial by Wilver, Summers and Cougle in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology assigned 84 undergraduate women with elevated appearance concerns to either two weeks of daily text reminders to reduce appearance-related safety behaviors such as mirror checking and grooming, or to no instruction. At post-treatment and two-week follow-up, the reminder group had lower social anxiety, BDD symptoms, body dissatisfaction and maladaptive cognitions than controls [3]. The authors argued the results support a role for these behaviors in maintaining BDD and related concerns [3].
No studies found that examine mirror checking or avoidance specifically within looksmaxxing communities.

quick.overview:
Mirror checking means repeatedly inspecting one's appearance; mirror avoidance means steering clear of mirrors. Both are described in body dysmorphic disorder.

Sources specific to how these habits appear in looksmaxxing culture are thin.
quick.mechanism: In BDD they are treated as rituals that maintain preoccupation; CBT with exposure and response prevention targets them.
quick.risks: They are described as time-consuming and linked to distress in BDD; clinicians evaluate them as part of diagnosis.
